faq.answer: No. Legal duty, discrimination, union work, community survival, family responsibility, or an explicit request may require advocacy. Examine authorization and power distribution.
faq.question: Does advocacy prove a social Eight subtype?

faq.answer: Requested protection begins with affected people’s stated needs and preserves their decision power. Self-appointed action may impose risk or silence the people it claims to defend.
faq.question: Why distinguish requested from self-appointed protection?

faq.answer: Following a less powerful member’s plan, accepting correction, and returning authority after the threat ends weaken an account centered on retaining protective group power.
faq.question: What leadership handoff weakens the social hypothesis?

sections.body_md: The tradition suggests that direct force may be organized around allies, vulnerable members, or a collective cause. Observe authorization, benefit, accountability, and whether power returns to the group.
sections.title: Frame group protection as a proposed autonomy route

sections.body_md: Social instinct is a traditional observation label, not evidence about bodily mechanisms. Law, discrimination, governance, collective bargaining, and public safety require their own evidence.
sections.title: Keep social language at the role-and-attention level

sections.body_md: Hold the threat constant and compare an intervention requested by affected members with one initiated without consultation. Record voice gained, resources transferred, risk imposed, and recourse.
sections.title: Compare requested and self-appointed protection

sections.body_md: Protection may appear as direct challenge, legal organizing, resource distribution, mentoring, or building durable group procedures. Loud advocacy is only one possible surface.
sections.title: Allow visible confrontation or quiet infrastructure

sections.body_md: Union office, safeguarding responsibility, emergency command, civil-rights work, family role, persecution, and absent public services may require collective protection independent of subtype.
sections.title: Audit duty, discrimination, and institutional failure

sections.body_md: Confidence falls when the person declines spokesperson status, follows the group’s chosen strategy, accepts correction from less powerful members, and releases control after the threat is contained.
sections.title: Look for power returned to affected members

sections.body_md: The subtype cannot establish fairness, loyalty, political correctness, or leadership legitimacy. Instrument-specific findings do not prove a universal ontology, and outcomes must be evaluated directly.
sections.title: Do not infer justice or moral authority

sections.body_md:
Duration: 4

Context: Across four days, examine one protective group action and one routine governance decision involving the same affected members.

Observable signal: Record who requested action, who spoke, who bore risk, resources transferred, dissent allowed, decision power gained, and when leadership was released.

Page-specific signal: Compare protection that increases affected members’ agency with intervention that centralizes authority in the protector.

Alternative explanation: Check formal safeguarding duty, union role, discrimination, institutional failure, persecution, emergency command, and family expectations.

Reflection prompt: Identify the event where following the group’s strategy worked best and revise any self-appointed-protection interpretation.

seo.description: Type Eight social is a traditional, evidence-limited hypothesis combining Type Eight autonomy with solidarity, protection, group power, justice, loyalty, and collective action. Advocacy does not establish subtype because professional duty, discrimination, union roles, community defense, institutional failure, political conditions, and direct requests from affected people can produce similar behavior.
seo.title: Type Eight social: a solidarity, protection, and group-power hypothesis
